title: Workflow, zoning and people management
audience: Trainee or new worker on the pressure cleaning (all heights) track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Plan safe zones, surface sequence, runoff controls, spot-testing, protected equipment and pedestrian interfaces.

instruction.heading: Plan the zones before the first pass
instruction.body: A pressure job is easier to control when the site is divided into zones before the first pass. Mark the spray zone, where the jet and the overspray go. Mark the exclusion zone, which is the wider area that people and animals must stay out of. Mark the equipment zone, where the machine, the pump, the fuel and the power connection sit, and keep it outside the spray. Mark the runoff zone, where the wash water will go, and the access route for people and vehicles. Sketch the zones on a site plan and walk them with the team before setup. The plan should be changed when the site changes, and the change should be briefed to everyone who is on site. A zone that exists only in the operator's head is not a control.

instruction.heading: Surface sequence
instruction.body: Plan the order in which surfaces are cleaned. The sequence should suit the material and the risk to the surface, and it should keep finished areas from being re-soiled by water running off untreated areas. A common working practice is to work from the higher surfaces down, so that runoff from upper areas does not wash over surfaces already cleaned. This is working practice, not a legal requirement, and it must give way to the surface test and the owner's instructions. Where a surface is fragile, it may need manual or low-pressure cleaning, and it may be left until last or handled separately. Record the sequence on the site plan so that the team and the owner can see it.

instruction.heading: Spot-testing and trial areas
instruction.body: Before a method is used across a surface, test it on a small area that is hidden or otherwise unimportant. Start with the least forceful method and the lowest effective setting the manufacturer's data allows, then increase only if the surface has not reacted. Record the location, the method, the result and the time of the test. If the test causes damage, stop, record it, and change the method or refer the surface to a specialist. Do not widen the method to a larger area until the test result is accepted by the owner. A test on one material does not cover another material on the same building, so each material needs its own test.

instruction.heading: Runoff, wastewater and stormwater
instruction.body: Plan the runoff before the water is used. The Victorian EPA guide on stormwater pollution, dated August 2007, says the runoff of wastewater and liquid or solid waste into the stormwater system must be avoided. Practical controls include sweeping before wetting, dry-cleaning where the surface allows, directing runoff onto the lawn or a soil area where that is permitted, and capturing the wastewater with a barrier or a sump. For yard and workshop wet cleaning, the same guide says wastewater should go to sewer through a water and oil separator under a trade waste agreement. Do not add detergent to a stormwater path, and do not let runoff reach a drain or a waterway because it seemed too small to matter.

instruction.heading: Protected equipment and electrical equipment
instruction.body: Protect what the spray can damage. Cover or shield vehicles, plants, windows, light fittings, meters, letterboxes, electrical outlets and any exposed fixture before work starts. Keep electrical equipment away from water. The Queensland safety alert says equipment used near water should be connected to a safety switch or residual current device, or fitted with a portable RCD, and that cords should be kept off the ground so they do not contact water. Route the hose and the cord so that they do not cross the exclusion zone or a walkway, and so that nobody can trip on them.

instruction.heading: Pedestrians and the team
instruction.body: The pedestrian interface is the edge of the exclusion zone, and it needs a person who controls it. Put a spotter at the edge where the public can reach the zone, with a clear instruction to stop work when someone enters. Use barrier tape, cones and signs to show the route around the zone. Brief the team at the start of each shift on the zones, the stop triggers and each person's role. Operators, spotters and any helpers must know who makes the stop decision. Where work is above ground level, the fall controls in Safe Work Australia's control order apply, and the work must stay on the ground or solid construction where possible. Noise from the equipment affects the team and the public, and the exposure standard for workers is 85 decibels as an average over eight hours. Rotate operators where the noise and the work load require it, and record the rotation.

instruction.heading: Handover and records
instruction.body: At the end of each stage, record what was cleaned, what was not, what was tested, where the runoff went, and any damage or near miss. Hand over the site to the owner or the supervisor with the exclusions and the open items written down. A handover that is only spoken is hard to check later.

procedure: Draw the site plan with the spray zone, exclusion zone, equipment zone, runoff zone and access route marked.
Brief the team on the zones, the stop triggers, the roles of each person and who makes the stop decision.
Plan the surface sequence and record it on the plan, and identify fragile surfaces that need a different method.
Spot-test each material on a hidden or unimportant area, and record the location, method and result before wider use.
Plan the runoff route and the containment, and check the stormwater path before the water is used.
Protect vehicles, plants, windows, fixtures and electrical equipment, and route the hose and cord clear of walkways.
Place a spotter at the edge of the exclusion zone where the public can reach it, and set the barrier and signs.
Record the work, the test results, the runoff route and any damage at the end of each stage, and hand over with the open items written down.

workedExamples.situation: A row of parked cars sits at the kerb, close to a footpath used by school students. The spray will reach the footpath and the car bonnets. This is an example job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you zone and protect the area, and when do you stop?
workedExamples.reasoning: Mark the exclusion zone to include the footpath section the spray can reach, and place a spotter at its edge. Cover or move the cars where the owner agrees, and protect the bonnets that cannot be moved. Reposition the operator so the spray goes away from the footpath. Stop whenever a student or a passer-by enters the zone, and restart only when the zone is clear again. Record the decision and the spotter's name.

workedExamples.situation: The planned runoff from a driveway would flow to a stormwater grate at the kerb. The owner has asked for the driveway to be washed. This is an example job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do before using water on the driveway?
workedExamples.reasoning: Sweep the driveway first and dry-clean wherever the surface allows, so less material goes into the water. Set a barrier or a sump so that the wastewater is held and does not reach the grate. If the wastewater cannot be contained, stop and refer the job, and record the decision. Do not add detergent that would run into the grate.

workedExamples.situation: A spot test on a hidden area of a painted wall shows the paint lifting. The owner wants the rest of the wall done today. This is an example job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the wall be done with the same method?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The test shows the method damages this material, so stop, record the test and its location, and change the method or refer the wall to a specialist. Do not widen the method to the wall until the owner has accepted a new method. Record the owner's decision in writing.

equipmentAndPpe: Site plan with the zones marked, printed or on a tablet
Barrier tape, cones and signs for the exclusion zone and the access route
Protective sheeting, covers and masking for vehicles, plants and fixtures
Sweeping tools and a containment barrier or sump for runoff
Portable RCD or a safety switch for electrical equipment used near water
Two-way radios or another agreed signal between the operator and the spotter
Closed footwear, high-visibility clothing for the spotter, and hearing protection where noise cannot be controlled
First-aid kit and emergency contact list on site

commonErrors.error: Starting the work without a zone plan.
commonErrors.prevention: Draw and brief the zones before setup, and change the plan when the site changes.

commonErrors.error: Working lower surfaces first, so that runoff re-soils cleaned areas.
commonErrors.prevention: Plan the sequence from the higher surfaces down, as a working practice, and give way to the surface test.

commonErrors.error: Skipping the spot test because the surface looks similar to the last job.
commonErrors.prevention: Test each material on a hidden or unimportant area, and record the result.

commonErrors.error: Letting wash water run into a stormwater drain.
commonErrors.prevention: Sweep first, contain the runoff, and check the local rules before the water is used.

commonErrors.error: Leaving the public unmanaged at the edge of the exclusion zone.
commonErrors.prevention: Post a spotter with a stop instruction, and brief the team on who makes the stop decision.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Stormwater: the 2007 Victorian EPA guide says wastewater and liquid waste must not run into the stormwater system. That guide is historical.

Electrical equipment near water: a safety switch or portable RCD, with the cord kept off the ground, is recommended by the Queensland alert, which concerns inflatable balls and is applied here by analogy.

Height: where the work is above ground level, Safe Work Australia's control order applies, starting with work on the ground or a solid construction. The elevated-work licence positions are set out in the first lesson of this course, Scope and surface survey, and are not repeated here.
Noise: the exposure standard for workers is 85 decibels as an average over eight hours.
Completing this lesson does not give authority for any licensed or regulated task, including work at height, electrical work or regulated jetting.

qualityStandard: The site plan shows the spray, exclusion, equipment, runoff and access zones, and it is briefed to the team before setup.
Each material has a recorded spot test before wider use, and damage stops the wider method.
Runoff is contained or routed as the local rules allow, and no wastewater is released to stormwater.
A spotter controls the pedestrian interface, and the team knows who makes the stop decision.
documentationEvidence: Site plan with the zones, the sequence, the access route and the runoff route marked
Spot-test log with the location, method, result and time
Runoff control record, with any local rule checked and its source
Team briefing record with each person's role and stop authority
Handover record with the open items and any damage or near miss
summary: Zone the site before the first pass: spray, exclusion, equipment, runoff and access.
Plan the sequence, spot-test each material, and stop and change the method if a test causes damage.
Contain the runoff, keep electrical equipment and cords clear of water, and protect vehicles and fixtures.
A spotter controls the pedestrian edge, and the team knows who makes the stop decision.

knowledgeChecks.question: What should be planned before the first pass on a pressure cleaning job?
options: Only the price of the job, the quote, the client's name and address, and the date of the invoice to be sent
The spray, exclusion, equipment, runoff and access zones, the sequence, the spot test, and the pedestrian edge
Only the equipment list for the crew and the van, its supplies, and the fuel for the whole job
Nothing, if the site is small and the job is quick to do for the owner and the client, since the work is simple

knowledgeChecks.question: A spot test on a hidden area shows damage. What is correct?
options: Continue at the same setting, since the damage is only small
Stop, record the test, and change the method or refer the surface
Test a larger area to see if the damage spreads across the surface
Hide the damage with a cover and continue with the job as planned

knowledgeChecks.question: Wash water is heading toward a stormwater drain. What is correct?
options: Let it run, because it is only water and it will soak away quickly
Contain or divert the runoff and check the local rules before continuing
Add detergent to speed up the wash and clear the drain fast
Pour the water down the drain to keep the path clear for the crew today
